title: Inspecting and Forwarding Mixin Content
learning_outcomes: Explain inspecting and forwarding mixin content and connect it to at least two of its syllabus subtopics.
Apply inspecting and forwarding mixin content in a small SCSS example and predict the resulting CSS or compiler behavior.
Inspect the output, diagnose one plausible mistake, and state a relevant limitation or best practice.

content.intro: This lesson turns **Inspecting and Forwarding Mixin Content** into a practical, inspectable step. You will connect content-existence checks with forwarding arguments to nested mixins, then check what Dart Sass emits instead of relying on the SCSS source alone.
content.why_it_matters: A mixin packages a reusable group of declarations or nested rules. Parameters make the intended variation explicit, while `@content` lets the caller supply a controlled block when a wrapper needs caller-owned styles.

content_blocks.title: The mental model
content_blocks.text: Give each mixin one clear purpose, document arguments and defaults, and check for repeated declarations when it is included in many components. Prefer a plain class or a function when it communicates intent more directly.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Start with the smallest source file that demonstrates inspecting and forwarding mixin content. 2. State what should change and what should stay the same. 3. Compile the entrypoint with Dart Sass, or use the stated command if this lesson is about the toolchain. 4. Compare the resulting CSS or diagnostic with the expected result, then change one input and repeat.

content_blocks.title: Inspectable example: Inspecting and Forwarding Mixin Content
content_blocks.code:
@mixin flex-center { display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; }
.dialog { @include flex-center; }
content_blocks.expected_output: .dialog { display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; }
content_blocks.execution_note: This course example is a Sass/SCSS or tooling example. CodeLeaf’s current in-browser playground previews HTML/CSS/JavaScript only; compile Sass locally with Dart Sass. Do not treat the browser preview as a Sass compiler.

content_blocks.title: Modern Sass note
content_blocks.text: Use Dart Sass for new work. Prefer @use / @forward and namespaced sass: built-in modules. Sass compiles to CSS; browser-native CSS features still run in the browser.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a small SCSS example that demonstrates inspecting and forwarding mixin content. Keep the example focused on one behavior, compile it with the version used by your project, and explain which part of the output proves your understanding.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake to avoid
content_blocks.text: Do not edit generated CSS when you intend to change source behavior. Edit the SCSS entrypoint or its module, compile again, and compare the generated output.

task_acceptance_criteria: The example includes the intended Sass construct and a clear input.
The expected output or tool result is documented and consistent with the source.
The work is reproducible and includes one limitation, test, or troubleshooting note.
hints: Reduce the example to one source file and one entrypoint before adding more abstractions.
Read the first compiler diagnostic and confirm you are editing the Sass source, not only generated CSS.
Compile and inspect the emitted CSS; compare exact selectors, values, and at-rules with your expectation.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming SCSS runs directly in the browser.
common_mistakes.why: Browsers consume CSS, not Sass syntax.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile with Dart Sass and load the resulting .css file in the HTML page.

common_mistakes.problem: Trusting source readability without inspecting generated output.
common_mistakes.why: Nesting, mixins, loops, and extension can emit unexpected selectors or more CSS than intended.
common_mistakes.fix: Compile a small example and inspect the CSS output or browser computed styles.
